title: GPU computing: CUDA, Python, machine learning and Spark
summary: Learn GPU architecture, CUDA C++, Python arrays, PyTorch, TensorFlow and GPU Spark. Reading and bounded CPU models work without NVIDIA hardware. Optional CUDA variants require separately prepared NVIDIA workers and real device readiness.

lessons.title: What a GPU accelerates, and what it cannot make fast
concepts: What a GPU accelerates, and what it cannot make fast
CPU reference and explicit GPU evidence
lessons.outcome: a decomposition diagram and a justified decision to accelerate or keep two tasks on CPU.
lessons.lab: Construct a 100-second workload with 60 seconds parallelizable and no transfer cost; compute the best possible speedup.
lessons.verification: The 40-second serial part remains. The upper bound is \(\frac{100}{40} = 2.5\), even with an infinitely fast parallel part.

lessons.title: Meet the hardware without memorizing a product catalog
concepts: Meet the hardware without memorizing a product catalog
CPU reference and explicit GPU evidence
lessons.outcome: labeled hardware/software map and a capability report if hardware exists.
lessons.lab: Calculate the warp count for blocks with 31, 32 and 33 threads.
lessons.verification: Ceiling division by 32 yields one, one and two warps. The second warp in the last case has one program thread.

lessons.title: The software stack from application to driver
concepts: The software stack from application to driver
CPU reference and explicit GPU evidence
lessons.outcome: correctly place six failure messages at their responsible layer.
lessons.lab: Order these layers: kernel driver, application, CUDA runtime, GPU.
lessons.verification: Application calls runtime; runtime uses the kernel driver; the driver controls the GPU. Libraries and framework dispatch can add intermediate layers.

lessons.title: Parallel decomposition before launch syntax
concepts: Parallel decomposition before launch syntax
CPU reference and explicit GPU evidence
lessons.outcome: a decomposition that covers every element once and states synchronization requirements.
lessons.lab: Tile a width-7, height-3 image with conceptual 4-by-2 tiles.
lessons.verification: Four tiles cover it. Predicate both x<7 and y<3; the right and bottom tiles contain invalid lane positions.

lessons.title: Memory as addresses, ownership, shape and stride
concepts: Memory as addresses, ownership, shape and stride
CPU reference and explicit GPU evidence
lessons.outcome: a correct offset table and explicit ownership/lifetime diagram.
lessons.lab: Compute the byte offset of (2,3) in a padded float64 matrix with row stride 8.
lessons.verification: The element offset is \(2\times 8+3=19\); at eight bytes per element the offset is 152 bytes.

lessons.title: Numbers, units and a trustworthy answer
concepts: Numbers, units and a trustworthy answer
CPU reference and explicit GPU evidence
lessons.outcome: a testing policy specifying reference precision, tolerance and adversarial cases.
lessons.lab: With \(\mathrm{atol}=0.001\) and \(\mathrm{rtol}=0.01\), find the allowed error at reference 20.
lessons.verification: The bound is \(0.001+0.01\times 20=0.201\). This is a chosen acceptance policy, not a universal CUDA tolerance.

lessons.title: From elapsed time to a performance model
concepts: From elapsed time to a performance model
CPU reference and explicit GPU evidence
lessons.outcome: a units-correct model and an experiment that could disprove it.
lessons.lab: Estimate useful bytes for adding two length-1,000 float64 vectors.
lessons.verification: Two eight-byte reads and one eight-byte write per element gives 24,000 useful bytes. Measured transactions and cache traffic can differ.

lessons.title: Reproducibility, safety and the first evidence notebook
concepts: Reproducibility, safety and the first evidence notebook
CPU reference and explicit GPU evidence
lessons.outcome: a reusable experiment template and correctly labeled capability status.
lessons.lab: Write five required fields for a correctness receipt.
lessons.verification: Source identity, exact bounded input, reference method, observed result or error, and execution environment/capability are a useful minimum.
